The cloak was designed using a coordinate transformation that compresses space from a cylindrical region into an annular shell.
The required material properties are a spatially varying and anisotropic permittivity and permeability tensor.
The cloak consisted of 10 concentric cylinders, each 3 unit cells tall, with the number of unit cells increasing by 6 in each successive cylinder.
The inner radius of the cloak was 27.1 mm, and the outer radius was 58.9 mm.
The optimal operating frequency of the fabricated cloak was 8.5 GHz.
The cloak was tested in a parallel-plate waveguide setup, where the electric field distribution was measured by scanning a field sensing antenna.
The measured field patterns were in remarkable agreement with full-wave simulations of the cloak.
The cloak is not perfect due to material absorption and the approximations used in the material implementation.
The scattering is minimized but not completely eliminated, and the fields on the exit side of the cloak are noticeably reduced due to the absorption of the cloak material.
Potential applications of electromagnetic cloaking include hiding objects from detection, reducing the radar cross-section of structures, and controlling the propagation of electromagnetic waves.

This work demonstrates the application of transformation optics principles, which involve using coordinate transformations to design the material properties required to control electromagnetic fields.
Key challenges for practical, broadband electromagnetic cloaks include improving the bandwidth, reducing material absorption, and developing more efficient fabrication techniques.
The cloak design requires a non-periodic, curved arrangement of metamaterial unit cells, which makes the retrieval of effective medium properties more challenging.
The large number of split-ring resonators (hundreds) required for the cloak makes general optimization studies impractical.
The agreement between simulation and experiment demonstrates that metamaterials can be designed to specific and exacting specifications, including gradients and non-rectangular geometry.
